book.title: Now, Discover Your Strengths
book.author: Marcus Buckingham and Donald O. Clifton

confidence_note: Definitions of talent, weakness and strength and the quotes on yearnings, rapid learning, satisfactions and losing track of time are from Goodreads quote pages of the book. Spontaneous reactions as a clue and the 34 themes come from Gallup summaries. Old flow framing, the one-week exercise and the accountant example were not in the book and were dropped.
facts: Knowledge is the facts and lessons learned; skills are the steps of an activity; talent is any recurring pattern of thought, feeling or behavior that can be productively applied.
Weakness: anything that gets in the way of excellent performance.
The acid test of a strength: the ability is a strength only if you can fathom yourself doing it repeatedly, happily and successfully; the goal is consistent near-perfect performance.
There is one sure way to identify your greatest potential for strength: step back and watch yourself for a while.
Spontaneous reactions provide the clearest trace of your talents; three more clues: yearnings (particularly when felt early in life), rapid learning, and satisfactions (the last clue).
Under satisfactions: see whether you become absorbed in the activity to such an extent that you lose track of time.
Excellent performers were rarely well rounded; on the contrary, they were sharp.

The Gallup profile asks you to choose between paired statements, reads instinctive reactions, and reports five signature themes out of 34 (e.g. Achiever, Activator, Empathy, Futuristic, Strategic); built from about 25 years of work and a little over two million interviews.
scene_details: a wish felt early in life
losing track of time inside an activity
pairs of statements to choose between
tension: Absorption is a clue to talent but only the last of several, and a strength needs more than being good.
opening_idea: Being so absorbed that time disappears, counted as the last clue.

lessons.idea: Test an ability against the book's wording: could you do it repeatedly, happily and successfully?
lessons.anchor: The strength test and the lose-track-of-time clue.

reflect_final: In the past month, which task made you lose track of time, and how much room does it have in your week?

use_cases.situation: A friend is choosing between two jobs
use_cases.move: Ask which tasks they could picture doing repeatedly, happily and successfully, the book's test for a strength.

use_cases.situation: You are splitting up a project among colleagues
use_cases.move: Ask who got absorbed in which task, the book's lose-track-of-time clue, before assigning.
Note which task made time vanish, as a clue rather than a verdict.

pocket_idea: A task that makes you lose track of time is the last of the clues to a talent, not the first.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Losing track of time is only the last clue to talent.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Talent definition, the three clues, the strength test.
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: good at it versus repeatedly, happily, successfully
